bull.argument: Costco's 2026 filing shows a business compounding on multiple fronts. Net sales rose 10% to $297,247 million, with comparable sales up 8% and digitally-enabled comparable sales up 21%, indicating strong member demand that is not just a gasoline story. Excluding gasoline price inflation, gross margin percentage rose 10 basis points to 11.22%, and SG&A as a percentage of sales fell 10 basis points, showing operating leverage. Membership fee revenue grew 11% to $5,907 million, and U.S. and Canada renewal rates held at 92.3%, which supports a recurring, high-visibility earnings base. Net income rose 14% to $9,226 million, or $20.76 per diluted share, and the Board approved a 13% dividend increase. The filing also notes that the company recovered tariff refunds and intends to reinvest most of them in member value, signaling management's pricing discipline. Risks are real, particularly the concentration in U.S. and Canadian operations and California, and the AI and cybersecurity exposures, but the financial results show a company executing well against them.

claims.claim: Comparable sales grew strongly, with digital growth well ahead of the total.
claims.quote: Digitally-enabled comparable sales increased 21% during 2026, both as reported and excluding the impact of changes in foreign currencies.

claims.claim: Membership economics are recurring and resilient, with high renewal rates.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

claims.claim: Earnings grew faster than sales and the Board raised the dividend.
claims.quote: Net income increased 14% to $9,226, $20.76 per diluted share, compared to $8,099, $18.21 per diluted share in 2025

bear.argument: Costco's own filing exposes concentration and fragility beneath the headline growth. The U.S. and Canadian operations generated 86% and 83% of net sales and operating income, and California alone is 26% of U.S. net sales, so a slowdown in one state could hit results hard. Much of the 10% sales growth leaned on gasoline: higher gas prices added $3,501 million, or 130 basis points, and the company itself notes that gasoline pricing inflates sales while lowering gross margin percentage. Gross margin percentage actually fell three basis points to 11.09%, and the 10 basis point improvement appears only after excluding gasoline. Membership fee growth of 11% was partly driven by a fee increase that accounted for roughly 30% of membership income growth, a one-time lift rather than durable demand. Management also warns that the business operates on very low margins, so modest cost changes can swing net income, and the filing flags rising healthcare and utility costs outside its control.

claims.claim: Gross margin percentage declined on a reported basis, and the improvement appears only after excluding gasoline.
claims.quote: Gross margin percentage decreased three basis points. Excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation on net sales, gross margin percentage was 11.22%

claims.claim: Sales growth was heavily boosted by gasoline prices, which the company says lowers gross margin percentage.
claims.quote: Higher gasoline prices positively impacted net sales by $3,501, or 130 basis points, with a 12% increase in the average price per gallon.

claims.claim: Membership fee growth was partly driven by a one-time fee increase, and the company operates on very low margins.
claims.quote: The fee income increase accounted for approximately 30% and 40% of membership income growth during 2026 and 2025.

bull.argument: The bear case is fair on concentration and gasoline, but it overstates the weakness. Gasoline added $3,501 million, yet comparable sales excluding gasoline and currency still rose 7% in the U.S. and 7% company-wide, so core demand is not a gasoline artifact. The reported 3 basis point gross margin decline is the gasoline mix effect the filing itself describes; excluding gasoline, margin rose 10 basis points to 11.22%, and SG&A fell as a share of sales. The fee increase did contribute roughly 30% of membership income growth, but that means about 70% came from new sign-ups and upgrades to Executive, and renewal rates held at 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada. Digitally-enabled comparable sales rose 21%, showing channel strength. Concentration in the U.S. and Canada is real, but California's 26% share of U.S. sales is a known exposure, not a hidden one. Management's thin-margin warning cuts both ways: it is why the company reinvests tariff refunds in member pricing, which protects the loyalty that drives renewals.

claims.claim: Core demand strength holds up after removing gasoline and currency effects.
claims.quote: Increases in comparable sales excluding the impact of changes in foreign-currency and gasoline prices (1) : U.S. 7 % 7 % 5 %

claims.claim: Gross margin ex-gasoline improved, and the decline reflects sales mix.
claims.quote: Excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation on net sales, gross margin percentage was 11.22%, an increase of 10 basis points.

claims.claim: Membership renewals remain high despite the fee increase.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

bear.argument: The opponent's rebuttal reframes the bear points, but the filing supports the caution. Comparable sales excluding gasoline and currency rose 7%, yet that is a company-defined adjusted figure, and the reported 8% includes the gasoline lift the filing says ran 12% higher per gallon. Calling the 3 basis point margin decline a mix effect concedes the point: sales growth is being bought with a lower-margin product line, and the filing states that higher gasoline prices negatively impact gross margin percentage. The 11.22% figure is a supplemental, non-GAAP view the filing itself says should be read alongside reported results. On membership, roughly 30% of fee income growth came from a price increase that is not repeatable at the same rate, and renewal rates fell to 89.8% worldwide, with the filing attributing pressure to online and international sign-ups. Digital comparable sales strength is real, but the filing says digital sales carry lower gross margin percentages, so that growth also dilutes margin. Concentration remains the core risk: 86% of sales and operating income come from the U.S. and Canada.

claims.claim: Reported gross margin fell, and the improved figure is a non-GAAP adjusted measure.
claims.quote: Gross margin percentage decreased three basis points. Excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation on net sales, gross margin percentage was 11.22%

claims.claim: Worldwide renewal rates are weaker than the U.S. and Canada figure the opponent cited.
claims.quote: At the end of 2026, member renewal rates were 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide.

claims.claim: Digital growth carries lower gross margin, so it does not fully offset margin pressure.
claims.quote: Gross margin is also impacted by our digitally-enabled businesses, domestically and internationally, some of which have a lower gross-margin percentage than our warehouse operations.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes from the filing and argue from them credibly. The bear effectively exposes that reported gross margin fell and that the margin improvement depends on excluding gasoline, and it responds to the bull's renewal and digital points with worldwide renewal and lower-margin digital evidence. The bull answers the gasoline and fee-increase concerns with reasonable counterpoints but leans on adjusted figures the bear successfully challenges, so the debate is closely balanced.
